entry:
Emergence of modern science in Europe during the 16th and 17th centuries. It was an irreversible break with the natural philosophy that preceded it, changing how the natural world was investigated and understood. The "New Science" departed from earlier Greek conceptions and traditions, was more mechanistic in its worldview and more integrated with mathematics, and focused on acquiring and interpreting new evidence. The period is often treated as a boundary between ancient thought and modern science.

It is frequently said to have begun in 1543 with the printing of *De humani corporis fabrica* by [[Andreas Vesalius]] and *De Revolutionibus* by [[Nicolaus Copernicus]]. Other historians propose 1572, when [[Tycho Brahe]] observed a supernova, as the starting point. The period is said to have culminated in 1687 with [[Isaac Newton]]'s *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica*. Johannes Kepler's laws of planetary motion, Robert Hooke's microscopy in *Micrographia* (1665), and the founding of the Royal Society of London (1660) and the French Academy of Sciences (1666) belong to the same period; the first scientific journal, *Philosophical Transactions*, was launched in 1665.

Much of the change in attitude is credited to [[Galileo Galilei]], whose telescopic observations provided persuasive evidence for heliocentrism and who developed the science of motion, and to [[Francis Bacon]], whose announcement of the progress of science inspired scientific societies such as the Royal Society.

The revolution built on earlier learning. Translations from Greek and Arabic into Latin, begun in the 10th century and accelerating in the 12th and 13th, together with the medieval university, supplied its foundation. Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler, and Newton all studied at universities founded in the High Middle Ages.

The term was popularized by the historian Herbert Butterfield in *Origins of Modern Science*. David Wootton calls the period the most important transformation in human history since the Neolithic Revolution.

Empirical method of acquiring knowledge through careful observation, skepticism, hypothesis testing, and experimental validation. Developed from ancient and medieval practices, it acknowledges that cognitive assumptions can distort the interpretation of observations. It has characterized science since at least the 17th century.

Inquiry typically involves forming a testable [[Hypothesis|hypothesis]] through inductive reasoning, predicting its logical consequences, testing it through [[Experiment|experiments]] and statistical analysis, and adjusting or discarding it according to the results. A hypothesis must be falsifiable: it must be possible to identify an outcome that conflicts with its predictions. Although often presented as a fixed sequence of steps, the method is better described as a set of general principles; not all steps occur in every inquiry or in the same order, and chance has played a role in some discoveries.

Early expressions of [[Empiricism|empiricism]] appear in the work of the ancient Stoics, Aristotle, Epicurus, [[Ibn al-Haytham|Alhazen]], Avicenna, Al-Biruni, Roger Bacon, and William of Ockham. During the [[Scientific Revolution]], [[Francis Bacon]] and Robert Hooke furthered empiricism, [[René Descartes]] described a rationalist approach, and inductivism rose to prominence through Isaac Newton and his followers. The term "scientific method" emerged in the 19th century, as institutional development of science and terms such as "scientist" and "pseudoscience" drew boundaries between science and non-science. It came into popular use in the 20th century; John Dewey's *How We Think* (1910) inspired popular guidelines. C. S. Peirce formulated the hypothetico-deductive model in the 20th century.

By the 1960s and 1970s, philosophers of science such as Thomas Kuhn and Paul Feyerabend had questioned its universality, favoring a view of science as heterogeneous and local practice. In *Against Method* (1975), Feyerabend argued against universal rules of science; Karl Popper and others disagreed. Lee Smolin's 2013 essay "There Is No Scientific Method" and Daniel Thurs's 2015 chapter calling it a myth or, at best, an idealization continue the debate.

European invasion, conquest, and colonization of most of Africa in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Seven Western European powers, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain, and the United Kingdom, contended for territory, driven by the [[Second Industrial Revolution]] and the era of "[[New Imperialism]]". The period saw a shift from "informal imperialism", meaning military influence and economic dominance, to direct rule.

As late as the 1870s, Europeans controlled approximately 10% of the continent, all of it near the coasts; the main holdings were Angola and Mozambique (Portugal), the Cape Colony (United Kingdom), and Algeria (France). Steamships, railways, and telegraphs aided expansion, and the development of [[Quinine|quinine]] as a malaria treatment made much of the tropics more accessible. By 1914 only [[Ethiopia]], later occupied by Italy in 1936, and [[Liberia]], which had strong connections with the United States, remained outside European control; Grokipedia-style estimates of about 90 percent colonized fit this picture.

Motives were economic, strategic, and political. Africa offered open markets during the Long Depression (1873–1896) and raw materials such as ivory, rubber, palm oil, cocoa, diamonds, tea, and tin. Britain wanted stopover ports on the route to India and the Suez Canal, completed in 1869, though historians such as John Darwin have challenged the theory that this drove its annexation of East Africa. John A. Hobson linked the period to shrinking continental markets, while William Easterly disputes a close link between capitalism and imperialism.

The Berlin Conference of 1884–1885, convened by [[Otto von Bismarck]] after claims in the Congo Basin by [[Leopold II of Belgium]], set rules for colonization, including "effective occupation", and excluded African representatives. Most colonies gained independence during the [[Cold War]]; in 1964 the Organisation of African Unity chose to keep colonial borders, fearing civil wars and instability.

Branch of the visual arts that operates in three dimensions, producing works with height, width, and depth. Durable sculptural processes originally used carving, the removal of material, and modeling, the addition of material such as clay, in stone, metal, ceramics, wood, and other materials. Since Modernism there has been almost complete freedom of materials and process, and works may also be assembled by welding, molded, or cast.

A basic distinction separates sculpture "in the round", which is free-standing, from relief, which is at least partly attached to a background surface and is classified as low or bas-relief, mid-relief, or high relief. Relief is the usual medium for large figure groups and narrative subjects and for architectural sculpture. Casting, stamping, and molding use an intermediate matrix and allow several copies. The term covers small works such as coins, medals, and figurines (normally no more than 46 cm tall) as well as colossal statues; the largest on record, the Indian [[Statue of Unity]], stands 182 m tall. Modern and contemporary art added sound, light, kinetic, land, and site-specific forms.

Sculpture in stone survives far more often than work in perishable materials such as wood, and often forms the majority of surviving works, apart from pottery, of ancient cultures. Most ancient sculpture was painted, and most of the paint is lost. It has been central to religious devotion in many cultures, and until recent centuries large sculptures were usually expressions of religion or politics. Small sculptures as personal possessions go back to the earliest prehistoric art, and public sculpture meant to impress with a ruler's power goes back at least to the Great Sphinx of some 4,500 years ago.

The Western tradition began in [[Ancient Greece]]. During the [[Middle Ages]], Gothic sculpture represented the agonies and passions of the Christian faith. The [[Renaissance]] revived classical models, producing works such as [[Michelangelo]]'s *David*, and the [[Baroque]] period brought dynamic movement. Modernist sculpture moved away from traditional processes and from the depiction of the human body, toward constructed sculpture and found objects presented as finished works.

Large body of salt water. The term has two meanings: the interconnected body of seawater spanning most of Earth, also called the [[Ocean|ocean]], and a named body of water, usually a marginal sea such as the [[Mediterranean Sea]] or a large, nearly landlocked body of water. There is no clear distinction between seas and oceans, though seas are generally smaller and often partly or wholly enclosed by land. The [[Sargasso Sea]], which has no coastline and lies within a circular current, is an exception, and the Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea states that all of the ocean is "sea".

Earth's 1,335,000,000 km³ of sea contain about 97.2 percent of its known water and cover approximately 71 percent of its surface. Another 2.15% of Earth's water is frozen, and the remaining 0.65% forms underground reservoirs or occurs in stages of the water cycle. Salinity varies widely, lower near the surface and at river mouths and higher in the depths, but the relative proportions of dissolved salts vary little. The most abundant is [[Sodium chloride|sodium chloride]]; seawater also contains salts of magnesium, calcium, and potassium, among others.

The sea moderates Earth's climate and plays important roles in the water, carbon, and nitrogen cycles. Winds blowing over the surface produce waves and slow, stable circulations; deep-sea currents, together called the global conveyor belt, carry cold water from near the poles to every ocean. [[Tide|Tides]], the generally twice-daily rise and fall of sea level, are caused by Earth's rotation and the gravitational effects of the Moon and, to a lesser extent, the Sun. Submarine earthquakes, volcanoes, huge landslides, and large meteorite impacts can cause destructive [[Tsunami|tsunamis]].

Bacteria, protists, algae, plants, fungi, and animals live in habitats ranging from the sunlit surface to the cold, dark abyssal zone and from polar ice to tropical coral reefs. Many major groups of organisms evolved in the sea, and life may have started there. Humans draw food, mainly fish, from the sea and use it for trade, travel, mineral extraction, power generation, warfare, and leisure; many of these activities cause marine pollution. Its scientific study is [[Oceanography|oceanography]].

Division of the year based on changes in weather, ecology, and hours of daylight in a given region. On Earth, seasons result from the [[Axial tilt|tilt]] of the planet's rotational axis, about 23.4°, relative to its orbital plane, together with the axis's approximately constant direction toward Polaris through the year. When the Northern Hemisphere tips toward the Sun, from around March 20 to around September 22, it receives more direct sunlight, with the maximum on about June 21; the Southern Hemisphere has the maximum around December 21. The two instants when the Sun is directly overhead at the Equator are the [[Equinox|equinoxes]], and the extremes of tilt are the [[Solstice|solstices]]. The low angle of the Sun in winter spreads incoming radiation over a larger area, and with shorter days this accounts for most seasonal climate variation. Because of seasonal lag, June, July, and August are the warmest months in the [[Northern Hemisphere]], and December, January, and February in the Southern.

Distance from the Sun is not the cause. Earth reaches perihelion in January and aphelion in July, and the effect of orbital eccentricity is a 7% variation in sunlight received. Proximity to oceans, ocean currents, latitude, and atmospheric circulation also shape local seasons.

Definitions vary with culture and region. In temperate and sub-polar regions, four seasons based on the [[Gregorian calendar]], spring, summer, autumn, and winter, are generally recognized. Ecologists often use a six-season model not tied to fixed dates: prevernal, vernal, estival, serotinal, autumnal, and hibernal. Many tropical regions have two seasons, a rainy or [[Monsoon|monsoon]] season and a [[Dry season|dry season]], and some add a third cool, mild, or harmattan season. Seasons may also be defined by ecological events, such as wildfire season. The ancient Egyptians recognized flood, growth, and low-water seasons, based on the annual flooding of the [[Nile]]; in India, six seasons, or *Ritu*, have been recognized from ancient times to the present for agriculture and trade.

Seasons hold special significance for agrarian societies, whose lives revolve around planting and harvest, and their change is often attended by ritual. In animals, seasonal changes in sunlight may prompt hibernation or migration, and plants may become dormant.

Principle of conducting human affairs on naturalistic considerations, uninvolved with religion. It is most commonly understood as the separation of religion from civil affairs and the state, and may be broadened to minimizing the role of religion in any public sphere. The term was coined in 1851 in Britain; "secular", like "religion", is a Western concept that is not universal across cultures, languages, or history. Secularism may encompass [[Anti-clericalism|anti-clericalism]], [[Atheism|atheism]], [[Agnosticism|agnosticism]], [[Naturalism (philosophy)|naturalism]], non-sectarianism, or neutrality on religion. It is concerned with minimizing the role of religion rather than disproving it, and may be hostile, neutral, or hospitable toward religion. People of any denomination can support a secular society, though secularist identity is often associated with the non-religious.

Distinct national traditions exist, including the French, Turkish, American, and Indian models. The American model emphasizes avoiding an established religion and freedom of belief; the French model is more interventionist. Scholars distinguish a strict form, associated with French *laïcité*, in which the state is officially distanced from all religions and non-religious convictions; a "humanistic" form, which seeks policy based on evidence and human welfare; and a "liberal" or "pillarized" form, common in German-speaking and Benelux states, in which governments may fund religions so long as they treat all convictions equally. In Indian political discourse, "pseudo-secularism" is a pejorative term for states said to favor one religion while claiming impartiality.

Principles associated with political secularism include legal equality regardless of belief, separation of church and state, state supremacy of the [[Rule of law|rule of law]] over canon law, freedom of thought, religious tolerance, and [[Reason|reason]] as a virtue. Supporters argue variously that it is a crucial element of modernization or the only guarantor of free religious exercise. Critics charge that it carries inherent bias against religion, citing state atheism under communist regimes, and that strict neutrality policies can clash with cultural religious practice. Some scholars suggest "post-secular" models, since religious influence is growing in some areas.

Plant structure containing an embryo and stored nutrients in a protective coat called a testa. Seeds are the product of the ripened ovule, after the embryo sac is fertilized by sperm from pollen to form a zygote, from which the [[Embryo|embryo]] develops and grows within the mother plant to a certain size before growth halts. Seed formation is the defining part of reproduction in seed plants, which now dominate biological niches on land, from forests to grasslands in hot and cold climates. Plants such as [[Fern|ferns]] and [[Moss|mosses]] have no seeds and propagate by water-dependent means. More generally, the term can mean anything that can be sown.

In [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]], the ovary ripens into a [[Fruit|fruit]] that contains the seed and disseminates it. Many structures called seeds are actually dry fruits; sunflower seeds are sometimes sold enclosed in the hard wall of the fruit. In stone fruits such as the peach, a hardened layer, the endocarp, surrounds the actual seed. Nuts are one-seeded, hard-shelled fruits, such as the acorn or hazelnut. In [[Gymnosperm|gymnosperms]], no special structure encloses the seeds, which begin development "naked" on the bracts of cones, although cone scales cover them in some species of conifer.

Flowering-plant seeds have three genetically distinct parts: the embryo, formed from the zygote; the endosperm, normally triploid; and the seed coat, derived from maternal tissue of the ovule. Development begins with double fertilization, in which two male gametes fuse with the egg cell and the central cell to form the primary endosperm and the zygote. The endosperm becomes the food the young plant consumes until its roots develop after germination. Ovules take four main shapes, anatropous, orthotropous, campylotropous, and amphitropous, and their shape often affects the final shape of the seed.

The first land plants evolved around 468 million years ago and reproduced by spores. The earliest seed-bearing plants were gymnosperms, which arose in the late Devonian period (416 million to 358 million years ago). Seed ferns followed in the Carboniferous period (359 to 299 million years ago), with ovules borne in a cupule of enclosing branches. Seeds underpin agriculture as the input for crop production.

Material with electrical conductivity between that of a conductor and an insulator. Its conductivity can be modified by adding impurities, a process called doping, and by electric fields, light, or heat. Raising the temperature increases conductivity, contrary to the behavior of a metal. Examples include [[Silicon|silicon]], [[Germanium|germanium]], gallium arsenide, and elements near the "metalloid staircase" of the periodic table. After silicon, gallium arsenide is the second most common semiconductor and is used in laser diodes, solar cells, and microwave-frequency integrated circuits. Silicon is critical for fabricating most electronic circuits.

The defining property in the Grokipedia-style band picture is the band gap, the energy needed to lift an electron from the valence band to the conduction band. For most semiconductors it ranges from about 0.5 to 3 eV; silicon's is 1.1 eV, germanium's 0.67 eV, gallium arsenide's 1.43 eV, and silicon carbide's 3.2 eV.

Adding a small amount, of the order of 1 in 10⁸, of pentavalent atoms (antimony, phosphorus, arsenic) or trivalent atoms (boron, gallium, indium) to silicon produces doped, or extrinsic, semiconductors. Group V dopants act as donors, creating free electrons ("n-type"); Group III dopants act as acceptors, creating free holes ("p-type"). Where regions of different doping meet in one crystal they form a p–n junction. The behavior of charge carriers (electrons, ions, and electron holes) at such junctions is the basis of the [[Diode|diode]], the [[Transistor|transistor]], and most modern [[Electronics|electronics]]. Devices can pass current more easily in one direction, show variable resistance, or respond to light or heat, and are used for amplification, switching, and energy conversion. In certain semiconductors excited electrons relax by emitting light, which is exploited in the [[Light-emitting diode|light-emitting diode]].

Some properties were observed in the mid-19th century and the first decades of the 20th. The first practical electronic application was the 1904 cat's-whisker detector, a primitive diode used in early radio receivers. Quantum physics led to the transistor in 1947 and the [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuit]] in 1958. The term is also used for materials in the insulation of high-voltage cables.

Biological system used by an organism to gather information about its surroundings by detecting stimuli, a process called sensation. Sense organs collect stimuli such as sound or smell and transduce them into a form the [[Brain|brain]] can interpret. Sensation and [[Perception|perception]] are fundamental to nearly every aspect of an organism's cognition, behavior, and thought. Some cultures traditionally identified five human senses, sight, smell, touch, taste, and hearing, but many more are now recognized, and the variety among non-human organisms is greater still.

A sensory organ consists of interrelated sensory cells that respond to a specific type of stimulus. Receptor cells, such as mechanoreceptors, photoreceptors, chemoreceptors, and thermoreceptors, transduce stimuli into action potentials. Signals travel through cranial and spinal nerves of the [[Central nervous system|central]] and [[Peripheral nervous system|peripheral nervous systems]] to the sensory cortices of the brain, where they are processed and perceived. Receptors can be classified by cell type, position, and function.

Senses are divided into external (exteroception) and internal (interoception) systems. Human external senses rely on the eyes, ears, skin, nose, and mouth, corresponding to the visual, auditory and vestibular, somatosensory, olfactory, and gustatory systems. Internal senses include proprioception (body position), equilibrioception, and nociception ([[Pain|pain]]), and further signals produce hunger, thirst, suffocation, and nausea.

Sensory modality refers to how information is encoded. Listing modalities, which can number as many as 17, involves dividing the major senses into submodalities. Touch, or somatosensation, can be separated into light pressure, deep pressure, vibration, itch, pain, temperature, and hair movement; taste into sweet, salty, sour, bitter, spicy, and [[Umami|umami]], each based on different chemicals binding to sensory neurons. Multimodality integrates senses into one perceptual experience, so that one sense can influence how another is perceived.

Other mammals generally have a stronger sense of smell than humans. Some animals detect electrical and magnetic fields, air moisture, or polarized light, or perceive through echolocation. Recent theory suggests plants and robots may detect environmental information in an analogous manner. Psychophysics, neurobiology, [[Cognitive psychology|cognitive psychology]], and cognitive science study the senses.
